n: T
The *Most High* is an ancient title that expresses the Lord’s exalted status as the ruler and protector of the godly (see {{Genesis 14:19|Genesis 14:19}}).
T
The Lord is an ancient shelter (see {{Psalm 90:1|Psalm 90:1}}), open to those who seek refuge in him.
T

This wisdom psalm expresses confidence in the Almighty God, who provides a shelter for those who take refuge in him. They receive redemption, life, and glory from the Lord, who loves and cares for those who seek him.
T
God protects the godly from deadly disease and even a destructive word.
T
The psalmist invites the godly to trust in the Lord and find protection in him.
T
The *shield* might refer to a large shield that covers the body. The *rampart* likely refers to a smaller shield, though the exact meaning of the Hebrew word is uncertain.
T
The godly should not be afraid, because the Lord watches over them. These promises do not guarantee an escape from trouble, but they create an expectation of the Lord’s goodness.
T
The word *pestilence* here means any kind of suffering or trouble.
T
The poet again invites the godly to seek refuge in the Lord and enjoy the benefits of divine protection.
T

*He will command His angels*: Satan quoted these words when he tempted Jesus ({{Matthew 4:6|Matthew 4:6}}; {{Luke 4:10-11|Luke 4:10–11}}). However, God makes this promise for those who obey him ({{Psalm 91:14|Psalm 91:14}}), not for those who arrogantly test him ({{Matthew 4:4|Matthew 4:4}}, {{Matthew 4:7|7}}).
T

Those who love the Lord will follow his commands ({{Deuteronomy 30:20|Deuteronomy 30:20}}; {{1 John 5:3|1 John 5:3}}) and look for his protection ({{Psalm 91:1|Psalms 91:1}}; {{Psalm 145:18|145:18}}).
T
The godly can trust the Lord’s protection and provision.
T

- The Lord promises to answer the prayers of his people. 

- The Psalms often mention people honoring the Lord ({{Psalm 50:15|Psalm 50:15}}). Here, God promises to honor the faithful who risk everything for him ({{Psalm 62:7|Psalms 62:7}}; {{Psalm 71:21|71:21}}; {{Psalm 84:11|84:11}}).
T
A long life on earth represents just a small part of the Lord’s goodness and eternal friendship ({{Psalm 23:6|Psalm 23:6}}).
T

In Jewish tradition, each day of the week has an assigned psalm: 

- Sunday ({{Psalm 24:1-10|Psalm 24}})

- Monday ({{Psalm 48:1-14|Psalm 48}})

- Tuesday ({{Psalm 82:1-8|Psalm 82}})

- Wednesday ({{Psalm 94:1-23|Psalm 94}})

- Thursday ({{Psalm 81:1-16|Psalm 81}})

- Friday ({{Psalm 93:1-5|Psalm 93}})

- Saturday, which is the Sabbath ({{Psalm 92:1-15|Psalm 92}})

This is the only psalm that indicates this use in its title.
T
The psalmist offers praise and thanksgiving for God’s loving devotion and faithfulness.
T

This psalm begins with thanksgiving and praise. The Lord, the Most High, is fair and just in judging the godly and the wicked. The godly will have a bright and strong future, while the wicked will die. 

Wise people see and understand the Lord's actions, which show his justice ({{Psalm 92:6-7|Psalm 92:6–7}}, {{Psalm 92:11|11}}, {{Psalm 92:15|15}}). The wicked, like grass, are quickly destroyed ({{Psalm 92:7-10|Psalm 92:7–10}}).
T
The Lord acts and the psalmist responds in praise ({{Psalm 92:4|Psalm 92:4}}). God’s actions come from his thoughts ({{Psalm 92:5|Psalm 92:5}}).
T
Fools perish because they do not understand the Lord’s great works and his eternal plans.
T
The Lord’s thoughts confuse those who lack understanding or act foolishly, and those who do not seek wisdom ({{Proverbs 1:22|Proverbs 1:22}}; {{Proverbs 10:23|10:23}}).
T
Even when the ungodly appear to thrive ({{Psalm 73:3-5|Psalm 73:3–5}}), they have no future ({{Psalm 92:9|92:9}}; see {{Psalm 1:6|1:6}}; {{Psalm 90:5-6|90:5–6}}; {{Isaiah 40:6-8|Isaiah 40:6–8}}).
T

The Lord is above the world of human experience. From this exalted place, he rules and judges ({{Psalm 7:7|Psalm 7:7}}). From there, he:

- celebrates his victories ({{Psalm 68:18|Psalm 68:18}}; see {{Psalm 47:1-9|47}}), 

- comes to rescue the needy ({{Psalm 102:19|Psalm 102:19}}), 

- brings an end to the wicked ({{Psalm 92:7-8|Psalm 92:7–8}}), and 

- receives praise ({{Psalm 148:1|Psalm 148:1}}).
T
The glory of the Lord is the reason the poet receives new strength and honor. It is also the reason the enemy will soon be defeated.
T
*like that of a wild ox*: The Lord allows the psalmist to express his joy ({{Psalm 92:8|Psalm 92:8}}). Because of this, the psalmist is strong and will overcome his enemies.
T
The psalmist understands the Lord’s mighty acts. He shares in the glory of the wise of heart.
T

Carvings of palm trees ({{1 Kings 6:29|1 Kings 6:29}}, {{1 Kings 6:32|32}}, {{1 Kings 6:35|35}}; {{1 Kings 7:36|7:36}}) decorated the temple. Builders used many cedars ({{1 Kings 5:6|1 Kings 5:6}}). The trees represent the godly, who are planted in the very courts of the temple.
T
The temple area consisted of the Lord’s own house and the courts that surrounded it.
T
*in Him there is no unrighteousness*: The Lord is always just. He rightly judges everyone (see {{Zephaniah 3:5|Zephaniah 3:5}}).
T
*robed in majesty*: The Lord stands victorious both before and after battle (see {{Psalm 45:3|Psalm 45:3}}).
T
The everlasting Lord gloriously establishes his kingship (see {{Psalm 47:1-9|Psalms 47}}, {{Psalm 99:1-100:5|99–100}}).
T

These psalms challenge the doubts created by the exile (see {{Psalm 89:1-52|Psalm 89}}) and answer the questions asked in {{Psalm 90:11|Psalm 90:11}}, {{Psalm 90:13|13}}. The Lord has established a kingdom ({{Psalm 93:1-5|Psalm 93}}) that is characterized by: 

- punishment of the wicked ({{Psalm 94:1-23|Psalm 94}}),

- respectful obedience among his people ({{Psalm 95:1-11|Psalm 95}}),

- justice for the poor ({{Psalm 96:1-13|Psalm 96}}),

- celebration in Zion ({{Psalm 97:1-12|Psalm 97}}),

- salvation for Israel ({{Psalm 98:1-9|Psalm 98}}),

- holiness ({{Psalm 99:1-9|Psalm 99}}), and

- praise ({{Psalm 100:1-5|Psalm 100}}).
T
God’s victory over natural chaos gives the psalmist confidence that the Lord will also defeat his present enemies (compare {{Jeremiah 46:8|Jeremiah 46:8}}; {{Jeremiah 47:2|47:2}}).
T

- Through his stable rule and royal laws, the Lord orders the world.

- *Your house*: The *house* from which God reigns might be the Lord’s heavenly palace or the earthly temple.
T
After the community suffers at the hands of the wicked ({{Psalm 94:5-7|Psalm 94:5–7}}), they pray for the Lord to bring justice (see {{Psalm 7:11|Psalm 7:11}}; {{Psalm 9:12|9:12}}).
T

This plea for the Lord’s justice includes both communal and individual expressions of sorrow ({{Psalm 94:1-7|Psalm 94:1–7}}, {{Psalm 94:16-23|16–23}}). The psalmist speaks about the pain and suffering caused by the wicked. He also describes the comfort and stability of the Lord’s protection. He calls on the Lord to avenge the needy against the arrogant and foolish, he rebukes such people for their foolishness ({{Psalm 94:8-11|Psalm 94:8–11}}), and speaks a blessing on the wise ({{Psalm 94:12-15|94:12–15}}).
T
When the Lord's enemies rise against him and his people ({{Psalm 3:7|Psalm 3:7}}; {{Psalm 93:3|93:3}}), he must rise and punish the enemy (see {{Psalm 79:12|79:12}}; {{Isaiah 65:6|Isaiah 65:6}}).
T
*widow … foreigner … fatherless*: The Lord’s law protects those in need ({{Deuteronomy 24:17|Deuteronomy 24:17}}; {{Deuteronomy 27:19|27:19}}), but they remain vulnerable in society.
T
The wicked think that they can get away with their evil acts and speech, foolishly assuming that God is not looking or does not care.
T
The writer of the psalm corrects people for acting foolishly.
T
It makes no sense for people who have ears and eyes to think that their Creator is deaf and blind.
T

*discipline*: This word can also mean "admonished" ({{Psalm 2:10|Psalm 2:10}}), "discipline" ({{Psalm 6:1|6:1}}; {{Psalm 94:12|94:12}}), or "instructs" ({{Psalm 16:7|16:7}}). The Lord disciplines his people to improve their character ({{Proverbs 3:11-12|Proverbs 3:11–12}}; {{Hebrews 12:6-11|Hebrews 12:6–11}}). He punishes his enemies by giving them what they deserve ({{Psalm 1:6|Psalm 1:6}}; {{Romans 6:23|Romans 6:23}}).
T
While the Lord’s thoughts are deep, people’s thoughts are worthless (compare {{Psalm 92:5|Psalm 92:5}}; {{1 Corinthians 3:20|1 Corinthians 3:20}}).
T
Because the Lord is faithful to his character, he rewards those who live by his wise instruction. He makes them happy, just as he promised.
T
God’s relief includes his comfort and rescue.
T
Even when it seems that he has, the Lord will not reject his people.
T
Only God has the power to stand up to the wicked (see {{Psalm 2:2|Psalm 2:2}}).
T
The psalmist resumes their prayer (see {{Psalm 94:1-7|Psalm 94:1–7}}) with a desperate plea for the Lord's justice. It ends with the hope that evil will cease.
T
The psalmist feels like he is slipping, but God promises to stand with him ({{Psalm 94:12-13|Psalm 94:12–13}}; see {{Psalm 15:5|15:5}}; {{Psalm 93:1|93:1}}).
T

This call to worship urges the people to respond to the Lord, the Shepherd, and to follow him faithfully. The previous generation, who refused to obey, did not receive the blessings of the promised land.
T
*above all gods*: The psalmist argues against idol worship and pagan beliefs ({{Psalm 96:4-6|Psalms 96:4–6}}; {{Psalm 135:15-18|135:15–18}}; see also {{Isaiah 46:5-7|Isaiah 46:5–7}}).
T
The Lord is the great King over the whole universe.
T
All creation exists because of the Lord alone, not because of many gods.
T

- The great King cares for his people like a shepherd cares for sheep ({{Isaiah 40:11|Isaiah 40:11}}). 

- The Lord, our Maker, the Creator of heaven and earth, also created a people for himself ({{Isaiah 45:9-12|Isaiah 45:9–12}}; {{Isaiah 51:12-16|51:12–16}}).
T

To *harden your hearts* means to be stubborn and resist the Lord's grace (see {{Numbers 20:2-13|Numbers 20:2–13}}; see also {{Matthew 13:3-23|Matthew 13:3–23}}; {{John 12:37-43|John 12:37–43}}; {{Ephesians 4:17-32|Ephesians 4:17–32}}; {{Hebrews 3:6-19|Hebrews 3:6–19}}; {{Hebrews 4:6-11|4:6–11}}).
T
If people want to enter into the Lord’s rest, they need to respond immediately (see {{Hebrews 3:7-4:11|Hebrews 3:7–4:11}}).
T
Israel's ancestors saw the Lord's wonders but did not understand their importance (see {{Psalm 92:5-6|Psalm 92:5–6}}).

- The generation of Israel that wandered in the wilderness for 40 years did not enter the place of rest that Israel enjoyed after conquering the land ({{1 Kings 8:56|1 Kings 8:56}}; see {{Deuteronomy 12:9|Deuteronomy 12:9}}). The Lord promised them the land and gave it to them ({{Isaiah 28:12|Isaiah 28:12}}), but they did not obey him ({{Isaiah 28:1|Isaiah 28:1}}). This warning reminds every generation of the need to obey with faith. 

- The rest that God provides includes peace, provision, and protection ({{Psalm 132:14-18|Psalm 132:14–18}}). The author of Hebrews challenged a new generation to enter the rest provided by Jesus Christ ({{Hebrews 3:7-4:13|Hebrews 3:7–4:13}}).
T

Three psalms begin by urging people to sing a new song ({{Psalm 96:1-13|Psalms 96}}, {{Psalm 98:1-9|98}}, {{Psalm 149:1-9|149}}). The song celebrates the Lord's universal kingship (see {{Psalm 33:3|Psalm 33:3}}).
T

- This psalm establishes the Lord’s universal kingship (see {{Psalm 93:1-5|Psalm 93}}) and prepares for the coming of the Lord to bring justice and righteousness to the world. The psalmist invites everyone to worship the Lord ({{Psalm 96:1-3|Psalm 96:1–3}}), the glorious Creator of the earth ({{Psalm 96:4-6|96:4–6}}), because only he deserves worship ({{Psalm 96:7-9|96:7–9}}). The universe joins in praise as the righteous Judge establishes a new order ({{Psalm 96:10-13|Psalm 96:10–13}}). 

- This psalm (along with {{Psalm 105:1-15|Psalm 105:1–15}}; {{Psalm 106:1|106:1}}, {{Psalm 106:47-48|47–48}}) is included in David’s song of praise recorded in {{1 Chronicles 16:1-43|1 Chronicles 16:1–43}}.

*great is the LORD … greatly to be praised*: The poet praises the Lord above all gods ({{Psalm 95:3|Psalm 95:3}}) and nations ({{Psalm 99:2|99:2}}). The Lord inspires more awe than anyone or anything else ({{Psalm 76:7|Psalm 76:7}}, {{Psalm 76:12|12}}; {{Psalm 89:7|89:7}}; {{Psalm 99:3|99:3}}; {{Psalm 111:9|111:9}}). He is beyond human possession or comprehension. The story of what he does to redeem his people causes them to praise him.

The gods of the nations are as nothing before the glorious and awesome Creator of the earth.
T
The Lord made the heavens, an even greater task than creating the earth. The idols, made by human hands ({{Psalm 115:4|Psalm 115:4}}), created nothing.
T

*Splendor and majesty*: The Lord is glorious ({{Psalm 96:6|Psalm 96:6}}; {{Psalm 104:1|104:1}}; {{Psalm 148:13|148:13}}), and so are his works in nature ({{Psalm 8:1|8:1}}) and in redemption ({{Psalm 111:3|111:3}}; {{Psalm 145:5|145:5}}).

- *families of the nations*: Families and clans represent subdivisions of the nations (see {{Genesis 12:3|Genesis 12:3}}). 

- The nations must respond to the Lord’s glory ({{Psalm 8:1|Psalms 8:1}}; {{Psalm 19:1-4|19:1–4}}; {{Psalm 24:7|24:7}}).

The courts of God’s sanctuary were usually not open to non-Jewish people. In this psalm, the nations of the world (people who are not Jews) are invited to come in ({{Psalm 65:4|Psalm 65:4}}; {{Psalm 84:2|84:2}}, {{Psalm 84:10|10}}; {{Psalm 100:4|100:4}}; {{Psalm 116:19|116:19}}; {{Psalm 135:2|135:2}}; {{Isaiah 1:12|Isaiah 1:12}}).
T

Worshipers should tremble in awe ({{Psalm 96:4|Psalm 96:4}}; see {{Psalm 18:7-15|18:7–15}}; {{Psalm 97:4|97:4}}) at the splendor of the Lord’s great power and holiness ({{Hebrews 12:25|Hebrews 12:25}}).
T

- The Lord’s coming means the end of injustice. He rules fairly ({{Psalm 9:8|Psalm 9:8}}; {{Psalm 96:13|96:13}}; {{Psalm 98:9|98:9}}). He brings a time of peace and order like the world has not known since Adam and Eve lived in the garden of Eden.

- The Lord’s rule over the world stands on the strong pillars of “righteousness and justice” ({{Psalm 89:14|Psalm 89:14}}), so it cannot be shaken (compare {{Psalm 11:3|11:3}}).

The psalmist urges all of creation to respond with joy to the news of the Lord’s coming. Compare a similar theme in {{Psalm 98:7-9|Psalm 98:7–9}}.
T

All of nature will experience renewal in God’s presence ({{Psalm 65:13|Psalms 65:13}}; {{Psalm 72:6|72:6}}, {{Psalm 72:16|16}}; {{Isaiah 44:23|Isaiah 44:23}}; {{Isaiah 55:12|55:12}}; {{Romans 8:21-22|Romans 8:21–22}}).
T
The *distant shores* represent the most remote parts of the world.
T

God is greatly exalted over the gods and over all the earth. Awe-inspiring phenomena accompany his coming. Even the created order is visibly affected and the wicked perish, but the people of Zion love his coming and rejoice.
T
*Clouds … Fire … lightning*: This language shows that the Lord is coming to judge.
T
All creation responds to the coming of its King. He alone deserves worship.

- When the Lord comes into the world, the heavens announce his righteousness ({{Psalm 50:6|Psalm 50:6}}). 

- Every nation will see the clear display of the Lord’s glory (see {{Psalm 8:1|Psalm 8:1}}; {{Psalm 19:1-4|19:1–4a}}; {{Psalm 24:7|24:7}}; {{Isaiah 40:5|Isaiah 40:5}}).

At the Lord’s coming, when every god must bow to him, those who worship other gods will face their own foolishness (see {{Psalm 95:3-5|Psalm 95:3–5}}).
T
Jerusalem rejoices at the news of the Lord’s coming, for he brings justice and rescues the *upright of heart*.
T

Godly people who live with integrity (see {{Proverbs 2:7|Proverbs 2:7}}, {{Proverbs 2:21|21}}; {{Proverbs 3:32|3:32}}; {{Proverbs 11:6|11:6}}, {{Proverbs 11:11|11}}; {{Proverbs 14:2|14:2}}) have hearts that are right before the Lord. They maintain a relationship with the Lord and live rightly with others ({{Psalm 94:15|Psalms 94:15}}; {{Psalm 125:4|125:4}}). 

The wicked plan to destroy the godly ({{Psalm 11:2|Psalm 11:2}}), but the Lord rescues them ({{Psalm 11:1|11:1}}; {{Psalm 36:10|36:10}}). Then the sorrows of the godly turn into joy and praise ({{Psalm 32:11|Psalms 32:11}}; {{Psalm 64:10|64:10}}; {{Psalm 111:1|111:1}}; {{Psalm 119:7|119:7}}).

This psalm celebrates the Lord as King. The Lord is the true King of Israel, its champion and savior. His people sing a new song to celebrate his victory and his faithfulness to them.

The Lord shows his righteous rule to all the nations of the earth. One day, this will lead to a worldwide kingdom of justice ({{Psalm 98:2|Psalm 98:2}}, {{Psalm 98:9|9}}). Because of this, all the earth should worship and rejoice together, for the Lord is coming ({{Psalm 98:4-6|Psalm 98:4–6}}).
T
The Lord makes known his righteousness and faithfulness (see also {{Isaiah 52:10|Isaiah 52:10}}).
T
The psalmist invites the whole earth to worship the King (see {{Psalm 96:1|Psalm 96:1}}).
T
The temple musicians played trumpets to gather people for meetings (compare {{Psalm 81:3|Psalm 81:3}}).
T
The psalm speaks as if all creation rejoices when the righteous Judge comes (see {{Psalm 93:3-4|Psalms 83:3–4}}; {{Psalm 96:11-13|96:11–13}}).
T

- It is appropriate to tremble and quake in response to the Lord’s holiness (see {{Psalm 96:9|Psalm 96:9}}). 

- The throne between the cherubim refers to the cover of the ark of the Testimony ({{Exodus 25:17-22|Exodus 25:17–22}}).

The Lord is the holy and righteous King ({{Isaiah 6:1-5|Isaiah 6:1–5}}). Mount Zion, where the temple of the Lord is located, metaphorically stands as the highest point on earth ({{Psalm 113:4|Psalm 113:4}}; {{Isaiah 2:2|Isaiah 2:2}}; {{Isaiah 6:1|6:1}}). From this high place, the "great King" ({{Psalm 47:2|Psalm 47:2}}) can see, rule over, and receive praise from all nations and peoples.
T
The psalmist calls the nations to worship the Lord, the king of the earth who rules from Zion.
T

The qualities of the Lord’s rule include: 

- strength,

- justice,

- love,

- fairness, and

- righteousness (see {{Psalm 93:4|Psalms 93:4}}; {{Psalm 97:2|97:2}}, {{Psalm 97:6-7|6–7}}, {{Psalm 97:12|12}}; {{Psalm 98:2-3|98:2–3}}, {{Psalm 98:9|9}}; {{Psalm 138:6|138:6}}).

Moses and Samuel were great models and leaders who had prayed on behalf of the Lord’s people ({{Exodus 32:31-32|Exodus 32:31–32}}; {{1 Samuel 12:23|1 Samuel 12:23}}).
T
God showed favor by responding to his people in the past, while holding sinners accountable.
T
The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron from *the pillar of cloud* ({{Exodus 33:9|Exodus 33:9}}; {{Numbers 12:5-6|Numbers 12:5–6}}). For a while, the people responded to the revelation.
T
This psalm calls all nations to come to Jerusalem to worship the Lord and acknowledge his goodness to Israel.

- The Lord is the one who determines who his people are.

- *the sheep of His pasture*: God will guide and protect his people ({{Psalm 23:1|Psalm 23:1}}, {{Psalm 23:4|4}}).
